p: In the autumn of thirteen forty-seven, Genoese galleys arrived at the port of Messina in Sicily, from the Black Sea, with dead and dying men at their oars. Within four years, the disease they carried had killed something like a third of the population of Europe, and perhaps a half; the Encyclopaedia gives estimates of between twenty-five and fifty million dead in Europe alone, and many millions more in Asia, the Middle East and North Africa. No war, no famine, no other calamity in the recorded history of Europe has killed so large a proportion of its people. Contemporaries called it the great mortality or the great pestilence. The name Black Death was given to it later.

The men of my own day do not know what caused it. Some speak of a poisoned air, a miasma, rising from corruption; that is what the physicians of the fourteenth century believed, and they ascribed the poisoning of the air to a conjunction of the planets Saturn, Jupiter and Mars in thirteen forty-five. The Encyclopaedia of the future tells me that the cause was found in eighteen ninety-four, at Hong Kong, by a Swiss-French physician named Alexandre Yersin, and the bacterium, a creature so small as to be invisible without a microscope, bears his name. It is a disease of rodents, especially rats and the marmots of Central Asia, carried between them by fleas. When the rats die, the fleas seek new hosts, and men will do. In its commonest form, called bubonic plague, the infection causes painful swellings, called buboes, in the groin, armpits and neck, with fever, vomiting and dark patches upon the skin; about half or more of its victims died, usually within a week. In another form, which attacks the lungs, it passes directly from person to person through coughing, and was almost always fatal. The men of the future have, astonishingly, recovered traces of the bacterium itself from the teeth of the dead in the plague pits of London and elsewhere, which settles the question of its identity beyond doubt.

It seems to have come from Central Asia, travelling along the trade routes of the Mongol peace. The Italian chronicler Gabriele de' Mussi told a dreadful story: that the Mongols besieging the Genoese trading city of Caffa, in the Crimea, in thirteen forty-six, catapulted the corpses of their plague dead over the walls, and that the fleeing Genoese carried the disease to Europe. The story may be true; it is more likely that the rats needed no catapult.

The accounts of those who lived through it are terrible. The Florentine writer Giovanni Boccaccio, in the introduction to his collection of tales called the Decameron, describes the city in thirteen forty-eight: the sick abandoned by their families, the dead piled in great trenches in layers like goods in a ship's hold, the breakdown of all law and custom, some people shutting themselves up and living abstemiously, others drinking and carousing day and night on the principle that tomorrow they would die. In Siena, a chronicler named Agnolo di Tura wrote that he had buried his five children with his own hands. In England the plague arrived in the summer of thirteen forty-eight and killed perhaps forty to fifty per cent of the people. Whole villages were abandoned, and you may still trace their outlines in the grass of the Midlands.

The horror bred cruelty. In many towns of Germany, France and Switzerland, the Jews were accused of poisoning the wells and murdered in their thousands, burned alive in their own houses or synagogues, despite the plain fact, pointed out by Pope Clement the Sixth, that the Jews died of the plague like everyone else. Bands of flagellants marched from town to town, whipping themselves bloody to appease the wrath of God, until the church condemned them.

Yet the historian must record, uncomfortably, that the plague had consequences that were in some ways beneficial to the survivors. With so many dead, labour was scarce, and the peasants and labourers who survived could demand higher wages and better terms. The lords and governments tried to hold wages down by law; the English Statute of Labourers of thirteen fifty-one forbade higher pay than before the plague. It did not work. The resentments it bred contributed to the Peasants' Revolt of thirteen eighty-one, when the rebels marched on London, and the priest John Ball preached on the text: when Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman? Over the following century, serfdom, the condition of peasants bound to the land and to their lord, withered away in England and much of Western Europe. Land was cheap and food plentiful for the survivors. Some scholars of the future have argued that this shift in the value of labour set Western Europe on a different path from the East, where serfdom grew stronger.

The plague returned, again and again, for three centuries. The last great outbreak in England was the Great Plague of London in sixteen sixty-five, described in the diary of Mr Samuel Pepys and, half a century later, in the Journal of the Plague Year by Daniel Defoe, the author of Robinson Crusoe. After that, for reasons still debated, it retreated from Europe. The men of the future report that it lingers still, in a few places, but can be cured by medicines of which I shall speak in their place.

I think the Black Death teaches us two things. First, that the civilisation of mankind has always been at the mercy of creatures too small to see, and that our trade, our cities and our travels, which are the glory of that civilisation, are also the highways of its destroyers. Second, that a society may be shattered and yet remade, and that the remaking may give the poor a little more than they had. I take no comfort in that. But I note it.
